title: Partition of Bengal
subtitle: Colonial reorganization, mass protest, and a new political fault line in Bengal.
summary: In 1905, the British colonial government partitioned Bengal and created the new province of Eastern Bengal and Assam with Dacca as its capital. Officials defended the move as administrative reform, but many critics treated it as a divide-and-rule intervention that weakened Bengali political influence. The measure triggered boycott campaigns, Swadeshi activism, new cultural forms of protest, and differentiated Hindu and Muslim political responses across Bengal.
heroTagline: What was announced as administrative reform became one of Bengal's most formative political ruptures.
whyItMatters: The 1905 partition matters because it transformed Bengal into a central arena of anti-colonial protest, sharpened debates over representation and communal interest, and helped reorganize the political language of boycott, provincial power, and community. Its effects extended well beyond the 1911 annulment into the deeper partition crisis of 1947.

historicalDebate: The strongest disagreement around 1905 is not whether Bengal was partitioned, but how to interpret the move and whose politics it empowered. Colonial officials described it as administrative reform, many anti-partition critics treated it as divide and rule, and historians note that Muslim responses were not identical to Hindu bhadralok opposition. The episode therefore matters both as an anti-colonial rupture and as a debate over representation, provincial advantage, and communal political differentiation.
